title: What crochet is, and where it came from
subtitle: A short history of the hook
excerpt: Crochet is fabric made with a single hook, one loop at a time. It is younger than knitting, it spread fast in the nineteenth century, and almost everything you can buy in a modern pattern traces back to a handful of stitches set down in Victorian needlework books.
sourceNotes: Historical outline drawn from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), and from the crochet sections of Weldon's Practical Needlework (1880s onward) and Caulfeild and Saward, The Dictionary of Needlework (1882). All public domain. The text here is an original summary in our own words, not a reproduction of those sources.

glossaryTerms.definition: A short rod with a hooked end, used to pull loops of yarn through one another. The single tool that defines crochet, as distinct from the two needles of knitting.
A style of crochet that builds pictures and lettering on an open square mesh by filling some squares solid and leaving others empty. Popular in the Victorian era for edgings and household linens.

content.text: Crochet is fabric made with a single

, working one loop at a time. You pull a new loop of yarn through the loop already on the hook, and the loops link into stitches. That is the whole idea. Because only one loop is ever live, you can stop mid-row, pull the work out and start again, or carry a project in a pocket without dropping stitches. This is the main practical difference from knitting, where many live stitches sit on two needles at once.

A handful of basic stitches do most of the work: the chain, the slip stitch, the double crochet, and the treble. Everything else is a taller version, a cluster, or a way of placing those few stitches. Once your hands know them, most patterns are just instructions for where to put each one.

Crochet is younger than knitting. It took its modern shape in Europe in the early nineteenth century and spread quickly through pattern books and magazines. For a while it was prized as a cheap way to imitate expensive needle lace, and fine cotton thread work flourished, especially the Irish lace that supported whole communities during hard years.

By the late nineteenth century the needlework manuals had set the stitches down in the form we still use. The names sometimes differed between Britain and America. That is why a British treble and an American double crochet are one stitch under two labels. Open mesh styles like
were used for edgings, curtains, and table linens right through this time.

Crochet survived because it needs almost nothing: one hook, one ball of yarn, and a few stitches. It is forgiving to learn, easy to undo, and quick to grow into something useful. The granny square, the dishcloth, the simple edging, and the baby blanket have all stayed in steady use for well over a century because the basic skill carries straight across them.

If you are new to the hook, learn the chain first, then the double crochet and the treble. With those three you can already make a scarf, a dishcloth, or a granny square. The stitch tutorials in this section cover each one step by step, and the foundation techniques cover counting, joining, and finishing. From there, almost any pattern is within reach.
